slides.title: The U.S. narrows its interests, puts the Hemisphere and economy first, and shifts burdens to allies

points.head: Stop treating everything as a national interest
points.body: Rejects post-Cold War strategies as wish lists; focuses on core interests only

points.head: Priorities: borders, burden-shifting, economic security
points.body: End of mass migration, allies paying more, reindustrialization, energy, balanced trade

points.head: The Hemisphere comes first; Asia is about economics and deterrence
points.body: A “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine; rebalance with China and deter along the First Island Chain

points.head: Allies must carry their regions; NATO is held to 5% of GDP on defense
points.body: Japan and South Korea are urged to spend more and invest in First Island Chain capabilities

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.1–29

slides.title: It dismisses post-Cold War strategies as wish lists and insists on choosing

columns: Post-Cold War strategy (as the document sees it)

rows.label: Scope
cells: Aimed at permanent domination of the whole world

rows.label: Priorities
cells: Laundry lists of wishes; never defined what we want

rows.label: Allies
cells: Let allies offload the cost of their defense
Allies take primary responsibility for their regions

rows.label: Economy
cells: Globalism and “free trade” hollowed out the middle class and industry

rows.label: Institutions
cells: Tied policy to institutions that erode sovereignty
Defend sovereignty; reform institutions to serve U.S. interests

takeaways: Redefines strategy as a concrete plan linking ends and means
The rest follows three questions: what to want, what to use, how to connect them

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.1–2

slides.title: What the U.S. should want (ends)
slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.3–5

items.head: What strategy is: connecting ends and means

slides.title: Five core interests abroad; everything else comes second

cards.head: A stable Western Hemisphere
cards.body: Stable enough to prevent mass migration, cooperating against cartels, free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets

cards.head: The Indo-Pacific and the economy
cards.body: Halt damage to the U.S. economy; keep the Indo-Pacific free and open, sea lanes navigable and supply chains secure

cards.head: Freedom and security in Europe
cards.body: Support allies in Europe's security while restoring its “civilizational self-confidence” and Western identity

cards.head: No adversary dominating the Middle East
cards.body: Keep oil, gas and chokepoints out of adversarial control, while avoiding “forever wars”

cards.head: Technology and standards
cards.body: U.S. technology and standards, especially in AI, biotech and quantum, drive the world forward

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.5

slides.title: The aim is to tie together America's economic, financial, technological, military and geographic advantages

cards.head: Political system
cards.body: Still nimble enough to course-correct

cards.head: Economy
cards.body: The largest and most innovative; market access is leverage

cards.head: Finance and the dollar
cards.body: Leading capital markets and the dollar's reserve status

cards.head: Technology
cards.body: Underpins the economy and gives the military a qualitative edge

cards.head: Military
cards.body: The world's most powerful and capable military

cards.head: Alliances
cards.body: Treaty allies and partners in the most important regions

cards.head: Geography and resources
cards.body: Abundant resources, no rival power in the Hemisphere, oceans as buffers

cards.head: Soft power
cards.body: Unmatched cultural influence

cards.head: The people
cards.body: Courage, willpower and patriotism

slides.title: The strategy: principles, priorities, regions
slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.8–29

items.head: What strategy is: connecting ends and means

slides.title: Ten principles guide foreign, defense and intelligence policy, anchored in “America First” realism

cards.head: Focused national interest
cards.body: To focus on everything is to focus on nothing

cards.head: Peace through strength
cards.body: Strength deters, and lets the U.S. broker peace

cards.head: Predisposition to non-intervention
cards.body: A high bar for justified intervention

cards.head: Flexible realism
cards.body: Good relations even with different systems

cards.head: Primacy of nations
cards.body: The nation-state, not transnational bodies

cards.head: Sovereignty and respect
cards.body: No outside interference or censorship

cards.head: Balance of power
cards.body: No nation may dominate globally or regionally

cards.head: Pro-American worker
cards.body: Pro-worker, not just pro-growth

cards.head: Fairness
cards.body: No more free-riding or imbalances

cards.head: Competence and merit
cards.body: Competence underpins prosperity and security

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.8–11

slides.title: Five priorities: borders, rights, burden-shifting, peace deals, economic security

cards.head: The era of mass migration is over
cards.body: Border security is the primary element of national security

cards.head: Core rights and liberties
cards.body: Protect free speech and religion; hold abusers of power to account

cards.head: Burden-sharing and burden-shifting
cards.body: NATO's 5%-of-GDP Hague Commitment; the U.S. as convener and supporter

cards.head: Realignment through peace
cards.body: Presidential peace deals to extend influence and open markets

cards.head: Economic security
cards.body: Six pillars: balanced trade, supply chains, reindustrialization, defense industry, energy, finance

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.11–15

slides.title: It ranks the regions openly rather than treating every one alike

cards.head: Western Hemisphere: first
cards.body: A “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine: enlist friends, expand partners

cards.head: Asia: economics and deterrence
cards.body: Win the economic future, prevent military confrontation

cards.head: Europe: stand on its own
cards.body: Restore European “greatness” and primary responsibility for defense

cards.head: Middle East: shift burdens
cards.body: Shift burdens and build peace; no longer the constant priority

cards.head: Africa: from aid to investment
cards.body: Select partners; trade, investment, energy and critical minerals

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.15–29

slides.title: In Asia it rebalances economic ties with China while hardening deterrence along the First Island Chain

points.head: Rebalance the economy
points.body: Reciprocity and fairness with China; grow from $30T in 2025 to $40T in the 2030s

points.head: Pool allied economic power
points.body: Allies add $35T to America's $30T, over half the world economy; India and the Quad matter

points.head: Taiwan and the First Island Chain
points.body: Keep the declaratory policy against unilateral change; press allies to spend more and open ports

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.19–24

slides.title: In Europe, the Middle East and Africa, it shifts burdens to the region and pulls back

rows.label: Diagnosis
cells: Losing share of world GDP; warns of “civilizational erasure”
No longer the constant irritant it once was
Policy has focused on spreading liberal ideology through aid

rows.label: What the U.S. wants
cells: Stand on its own feet; a swift cessation of hostilities in Ukraine
Gulf energy, open Hormuz and Red Sea, Israel secure
Shift to trade and investment; energy and critical minerals

rows.label: Main tools
cells: Trade, arms sales; end the perception of NATO as ever-expanding
Expand the Abraham Accords; no nation-building wars
Partner with capable states; avoid long-term presence

takeaways: In all three, the region is expected to carry more of the load

slides.source: Source: U.S. National Security Strategy (Nov 2025), p.25–29

items.head: What strategy is: connecting ends and means

slides.title: Allies like Japan are asked for spending, capabilities, access and economic alignment

pairs.issue: Spend more on defense and on capabilities for the First Island Chain (Japan and South Korea named)
pairs.action: Check the effect on defense budgets, procurement and related industries

pairs.issue: Wider U.S. access to ports and facilities; a hardened Western Pacific posture
pairs.action: Map the effect on infrastructure, sites and logistics

pairs.issue: Countries that align export controls get better treatment on trade, tech and procurement
pairs.action: Review export controls, customers and technology partnerships

pairs.issue: Counter China's overcapacity; secure critical minerals and supply chains
pairs.action: Diversify sourcing; plan stock and substitutes for critical inputs
